thread.title: Trade And Legal Headlines Highlight Concerns For Apple, And Valuations Are Still Not Attractive - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)

author: Cloister Research
title: Trade And Legal Headlines Highlight Concerns For Apple, And Valuations Are Still Not Attractive - Apple Inc. (NASDAQ:AAPL)
text:
Apple ( AAPL ) investors were shocked (and Qualcomm (NASDAQ: QCOM ) investors delighted) to learn that a Chinese court had ruled against Apple in the ongoing dispute between the two companies. Qualcomm claims this ruling means that Apple must stop selling nearly all iPhones in China, while Apple claims that only older iPhones will be affected ( as reported by 9to5mac ). At writing time, the situation remains fluid, with conflicting takes on both sides. This ruling is only the latest in a spate of negative news flow for Apple, with concerns about iPhone sales mounting along with trade tensions between the US and a major piece of Apple's supply chain and global demand, China.
Indeed, despite recent hopes that the G20 meeting between President Trump and General Secretary Xi would cool rising trade tensions, markets were surprised again later in the week when Canada arrested the CFO of Huawei (the legendary Chinese mobile phone manufacturer, and direct competitor of Apple) for extradition and legal proceedings in the US revolving around Huawei's breaking of the US trade embargo on Iran.
As expected, Apple shares have been continually hammered on this and other news, with the stock falling from $232 to around $165, as of writing.
AAPL data by YCharts Is Apple, one of the bluest of blue chips, "on sale" at these prices, or is it not yet time to buy Apple? According to the work I've done below, Apple is becoming an interesting buy, but we haven't yet reached the point of calling the company undervalued .
Apple's valuation is not compelling today, even if the trade situation resolves amicably. For the first time in years, Apple has had a substantial share price pullback. Is the stock's valuation compelling today? With the stock trading down some 27% from its all-time highs, Apple just recently entered into a relative historical undervaluation, compared to its past two years.
Source: own calculations, company financial filings
Indeed, today shares trade at a > 2 standard deviation discount to its average price/earnings multiple over the past two years, as seen above. For those wishing to buy Apple, today's prices are a relative bargain over any time since December 2016.
Unfortunately, however, things are not quite as rosy if we include the prior two years - since the summer of 2016, Apple's valuation metrics have exploded, largely because of the new focus by management on the strength of its services segment and de-emphasis on iPhone sales growth. Including those lower-valuation days of Apple's prior life as a mobile phone company yields a much different picture.
Here we can see that Apple's recent price action is deceiving. Despite trading down 27% from its all-time highs, the equity is still trading near its average price/earnings ratio over the past four years. Although shares are certainly a more safe purchase today than they were only a few months ago, I would not be looking to add to a position until shares found their way ~20% or so lower from here, which would place the P/E multiple in the lower end of its historical range, where we would begin to say that the stock is undervalued.
Furthermore, with a dividend yield of only 1.73%, Apple is not yet attractive from an income perspective as well. With yields on two-year Treasuries nearly a full percent higher, it's hard to see any support from investors on a yield basis or as a defensive income play. Investors can simply go to short duration Treasuries, which have the dual benefit of a higher yield and a safer principal, particularly in times of market turmoil like we're experiencing in the past month.
The selloff in Apple's shares is justified Finally, I want to comment on the idea running rampant that the selloff in Apple's shares is not justified. On the contrary: This selloff was completely called for, due to a multitude of reasons.
Valuations were extremely stretched. As shown above, the shares of Apple were becoming extremely overvalued on a historical basis This alone was worthy of a 15% or greater decline, simply to bring valuations back to their (already fully valued) two-year average. Its principal product is in danger of decline. Despite reports to the contrary, Apple is and will be an iPhone company for the foreseeable future - not a wearables company, not a services company, and not a desktop company. Although conventional wisdom suggests that the company's future lies in its other bets, the percentage of the company's sales from its iPhones is actually increasing year-over-year. In FY2018, iPhone sales accounted for 62.8% of total sales, while in FY2017 they were 61.6% of sales. With numerous signs that sales of the iPhone will be declining in the next year (Apple will no longer break out iPhone sales, increasing trade-in incentives , etc), the company is in danger of its most important revenue line seeing stalling growth...or even decline. Tensions with China are growing. Of any country in the world (outside of the US), China is probably the most important with which to maintain good relations for Apple due to its dual roles as both a major supply chain component and a major consumer of Apple. With the US targeting Huawei (a substantial Apple competitor in China) with the recent arrest of its CFO, it's unlikely that China will neglect to retaliate; indeed, a Chinese court just happened to rule in favor of Qualcomm over Apple in their ongoing dispute this week. Apple is uniquely positioned to benefit from US-China cooperation, which also means that it's uniquely at danger when this cooperation is at risk of breaking down. With trade tensions flaring between the two countries, the risk to Apple's underlying business is beginning to become more than minor. Indeed, taking all of these major risks to the business and valuation into account, it's somewhat surprising to me that shares are only down 27% from their all-time highs. This is not to say that I'm bearish on the strength of Apple's business or products in general - the company still has an excellent ecosystem, strong products and brand loyalty, and a pristine balance sheet. However, valuations still look to be somewhat stretched from here.
Conclusion Despite Apple's recent substantial share price decline, the company is not yet a "must-buy" for investors. Substantial risks remain, including the company's not-attractive valuation, underlying iPhone sales trends, and continued trade tensions with China. For investors today, the shares are probably fairly valued, but I'm personally looking for a further decline of 20% before I add to my position.
